sources.entry: The State of Context Engineering summarizes the relevant approaches to context management: context augmentation, context quarantine, context summarization ("compaction"), tool loadout, context pruning, context offloading.

summary.title: The State of Context Engineering
summary.one_liner: Context engineering has moved from prompt writing to harness design, and the job is deciding what to make deterministic in code versus what to leave to the probabilistic model.
keywords: why do ai agents get worse over long sessions
how to manage llm context window
takeaways: Long context windows add more room for both useful and bad information; failures like poisoning, distraction, confusion and clash still occur.
Six context tools remain constant: augmentation, tool loadout, quarantine, pruning, offloading, and summarization/compaction, and are increasingly built into harnesses.
Agentic models can drift into context inertia, fixating on a subtask; periodically clearing context while keeping artifacts can help.
Models trained on specific harnesses can be biased toward their training tools and serial behavior, so prompts may need to fight the weights.
Output is the product of the weights and the context, so the design task is choosing when to be deterministic and when to let the model decide.
summary.summary: This is a transcript of a talk by Drew Breunig on the state of context engineering, covering how the field moved from the 2024 long-context push to today's agentic harnesses. He walks through four failure modes (poisoning, distraction, confusion, clash) with examples from Pokémon-playing Gemini runs and a research paper on instruction-following under contradictory examples. He then presents six context-management tools and shows, using a short DSPy example, how each can be implemented as simple code. The talk closes by describing newer failure modes such as context inertia and models overfitting to their training harnesses, plus a prediction about memory and skill accumulation in long-running personal agents.
